verses.zh: 保罗来到特庇，又到路司得。在那里有一个门徒，名叫提摩太，是信主之犹太妇人的儿子，他父亲却是希腊人。
verses.en: He also came to Derbe[NOTE:1] and to Lystra.[NOTE:2] A disciple[NOTE:3] named Timothy was there, the son of a Jewish woman who was a believer,[NOTE:4] but whose father was a Greek.[NOTE:5]
notes: Derbe was a city in Lycaonia about 35 mi (60 km) southeast of Lystra. It was about 90 mi (145 km) from Tarsus.map For location see JP1-E2; JP2-E2; JP3-E2.
Lystra was a city in Lycaonia about 18 mi (30 km) south of Iconium.map For location see JP1-E2; JP2-E2; JP3-E2.
Grk “And behold, a disciple.” Here ἰδού (idou) has not been translated.
L&N 31.103 translates this phrase “the son of a Jewish woman who was a believer.”

His father was a Greek. Timothy was the offspring of a mixed marriage between a Jewish woman (see 2 Tim 1:5) and a Gentile man. On mixed marriages in Judaism, see Neh 13:23-27; Ezra 9:1-10:44; Mal 2:10-16; Jub. 30:7-17; m. Qiddushin 3.12; m. Yevamot 7.5.

verses.zh: 路司得和以哥念的弟兄都称赞他。
verses.en: The brothers in Lystra and Iconium spoke well[NOTE:1] of him.[NOTE:2]
notes: For this sense of μαρτυρέω (martureō), see BDAG 618 s.v. 2.b.

Grk “who was well spoken of by the brothers in Lystra and Iconium.” Because of the awkwardness in English of having two relative clauses follow one another (“who was a believer…who was well spoken of”) and the awkwardness of the passive verb (“was well spoken of”), the relative pronoun at the beginning of 16:2 (“who”) has been translated as a pronoun (“him”) and the construction converted from passive to active at the same time a new sentence was started in the translation.

verses.zh: 保罗要带他同去，只因那些地方的犹太人都知道他父亲是希腊人，就给他行了割礼。
verses.en: Paul wanted Timothy[NOTE:1] to accompany him, and he took[NOTE:2] him and circumcised[NOTE:3] him because of the Jews who were in those places,[NOTE:4] for they all knew that his father was Greek.[NOTE:5]
notes: Grk “this one”; the referent (Timothy) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

Grk “and taking him he circumcised him.” The participle λαβών (labōn) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style. Paul’s cultural sensitivity showed in his action here. He did not want Timothy’s lack of circumcision to become an issue (1 Cor 9:15-23).
The verb περιέτεμεν (perietemen) here may be understood as causative (cf. ExSyn 411-12) if Paul did not personally perform the circumcision.
Or “who lived in the area.”

His father was Greek. Under Jewish law at least as early as the 2nd century, a person was considered Jewish if his or her mother was Jewish. It is not certain whether such a law was in effect in the 1st century, but even if it was, Timothy would not have been accepted as fully Jewish because he was not circumcised.tn The anarthrous predicate nominative has been translated as qualitative (“Greek”) rather than indefinite (“a Greek”).

verses.zh: 他们经过各城，把耶路撒冷使徒和长老所定的条规交给门徒遵守。
verses.en: As they went through the towns,[NOTE:1] they passed on[NOTE:2] the decrees that had been decided on by the apostles and elders in Jerusalem[NOTE:3] for the Gentile believers[NOTE:4] to obey.[NOTE:5]
notes: Or “cities.”
BDAG 762-63 s.v. παραδίδωμι 3 has “they handed down to them the decisions to observe Ac 16:4.”
For location see Map5-B1; Map6-F3; Map7-E2; Map8-F2; Map10-B3; JP1-F4; JP2-F4; JP3-F4; JP4-F4.
Grk “for them”; the referent (Gentile believers) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Or “observe” or “follow.”

verses.zh: 于是众教会信心越发坚固，人数天天加增。
verses.en: So the churches were being strengthened in the faith and were increasing in number every day.[NOTE:1]
notes: BDAG 437 s.v. ἡμέρα 2.c has “every day” for this phrase.

verses.zh: 圣灵既然禁止他们在亚细亚讲道，他们就经过弗吕家、加拉太一带地方。
verses.en: They went through the region of Phrygia[NOTE:1] and Galatia,[NOTE:2] having been prevented[NOTE:3] by the Holy Spirit from speaking the message[NOTE:4] in the province of Asia.[NOTE:5]
notes: Phrygia was a district in central Asia Minor west of Pisidia.

Galatia refers to either (1) the region of the old kingdom of Galatia in the central part of Asia Minor (North Galatia), or (2) the Roman province of Galatia, whose principal cities in the 1st century were Ancyra and Pisidian Antioch (South Galatia). The exact extent and meaning of this area has been a subject of considerable controversy in modern NT studies.
Or “forbidden.”
Or “word.”

Grk “Asia”; in the NT this always refers to the Roman province of Asia. The Roman province of Asia made up about one-third of modern Asia Minor and was on the western side of it. Asia lay to the west of the region of Phrygia and Galatia. The words “the province of” are supplied to indicate to the modern reader that this does not refer to the continent of Asia.

verses.zh: 到了每西亚的边界，他们想要往庇推尼去，耶稣的灵却不许。
verses.en: When they came to[NOTE:1] Mysia,[NOTE:2] they attempted to go into Bithynia,[NOTE:3] but the Spirit of Jesus did not allow[NOTE:4] them to do this,[NOTE:5]
notes: BDAG 511 s.v. κατά B.1.b has “to Mysia” here.
Mysia was a province in northwest Asia Minor.
Bithynia was a province in northern Asia Minor northeast of Mysia.
Or “permit”; see BDAG 269 s.v. ἐάω 1.
The words “do this” are not in the Greek text, but are supplied for stylistic reasons, since English handles ellipses differently than Greek.

verses.zh: 他们就越过每西亚，下到特罗亚去。
verses.en: so they passed through[NOTE:1] Mysia[NOTE:2] and went down to Troas.[NOTE:3]
notes: Although the normal meaning for παρέρχομαι (parerchomai) is “pass by, go by,” it would be difficult to get to Troas from where Paul and his companions were without going through rather than around Mysia. BDAG 776 s.v. παρέρχομαι 6 list some nonbiblical examples of the meaning “go through, pass through,” and give that meaning for the usage here.
Mysia was a province in northwest Asia Minor.
Troas was a port city (and surrounding region) on the northwest coast of Asia Minor, near ancient Troy.

verses.zh: 在夜间有异象现与保罗。有一个马其顿人站着求他说：「请你过到马其顿来帮助我们。」
verses.en: A[NOTE:1] vision appeared to Paul during the night: A Macedonian man was standing there[NOTE:2] urging him,[NOTE:3] “Come over[NOTE:4] to Macedonia[NOTE:5] and help us!”
notes: Grk “And a.” Because of the difference between Greek style, which often begins sentences or clauses with “and,” and English style, which generally does not, καί (kai) has not been translated here.
The word “there” is not in the Greek text, but is implied.
The participle λέγων (legōn) is redundant and has not been translated.
Grk “Coming over.” The participle διαβάς (diabas) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style.
Macedonia was the Roman province of Macedonia in Greece.

verses.zh: 保罗既看见这异象，我们随即想要往马其顿去，以为　神召我们传福音给那里的人听。
verses.en: After Paul[NOTE:1] saw the vision, we[NOTE:2] attempted[NOTE:3] immediately to go over to Macedonia,[NOTE:4] concluding that God had called[NOTE:5] us to proclaim the good news to them.
notes: Grk “he”; the referent (Paul) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

This marks the beginning of one of the “we” sections in Acts (16:10-17; 20:5-15; 21:1-18; 27:1-28:16). These have been traditionally understood to mean that the author was in the company of Paul for this part of the journey.
Grk “sought.”
Macedonia was the Roman province of Macedonia in Greece.
Or “summoned.”

verses.zh: 于是从特罗亚开船，一直行到撒摩特喇，第二天到了尼亚坡里。
verses.en: We put out to sea[NOTE:1] from Troas[NOTE:2] and sailed a straight course[NOTE:3] to Samothrace,[NOTE:4] the next day to Neapolis,[NOTE:5]
notes: BDAG 62 s.v. ἀνάγω 4, “as a nautical t.t. (ἀ. τὴν ναῦν put a ship to sea), mid. or pass. ἀνάγεσθαι to begin to go by boat, put out to sea.”
Troas was a port city (and surrounding region) on the northwest coast of Asia Minor. See v. 8.
BDAG 406 s.v. εὐθυδρομέω has “of a ship run a straight course” here; L&N 54.3 has “to sail a straight course, sail straight to.”
Samothrace is an island in the northern part of the Aegean Sea.
Neapolis was a seaport on the southern coast of Macedonia. It was 10 mi (16 km) from Philippi.

verses.zh: 从那里来到腓立比，就是马其顿这一方的头一个城，也是罗马的驻防城。我们在这城里住了几天。
verses.en: and from there to Philippi,[NOTE:1] which is a leading city of that district[NOTE:2] of Macedonia,[NOTE:3] a Roman colony.[NOTE:4] We stayed in this city for some days.
notes: For location see JP1-C1; JP2-C1; JP3-C1; JP4-C1.

‡ Or perhaps, “a city in the first district” (there are a number of textual variants). L&N 1.85 follow the text of UBS5 and NA28 here: “In Ac 16:12…the Greek New Testament published by the United Bible Societies has adopted a conjectural emendation, since the more traditional text, πρώτη τῆς μερίδος, literally ‘first of the district,’ is not only misleading in meaning but does not reflect the historical fact that Philippi was a city in one of the four districts of Macedonia but was not a capital city.” The Ausgangstext probably read πρώτη τῆς μερίδος (prōtē tēs meridos, “first of that district”) as found in P74 א A C Ψ 33vid 36 81 323 945 1175 1891. This has traditionally been translated to give the impression that Philippi was the capital city of the district, but it does not necessarily have to be translated this way. The translation of the article before μερίδος as “that” acknowledges that there were other districts in the province of Macedonia.
Macedonia was the Roman province of Macedonia in Greece.
A Roman colony was a city whose residents were regarded as Roman citizens, since such cities were originally colonized by citizens of Rome. From Troas to Philippi was 130 mi (208 km).

verses.zh: 当安息日，我们出城门，到了河边，知道那里有一个祷告的地方，我们就坐下对那聚会的妇女讲道。
verses.en: On the Sabbath day we went outside the city gate to the side of the river, where we thought there would be a place of prayer, and we sat down[NOTE:1] and began to speak[NOTE:2] to the women[NOTE:3] who had assembled there.[NOTE:4]
notes: Grk “and sitting down we began to speak.” The participle καθίσαντες (kathisantes) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style.
The imperfect verb ἐλαλοῦμεν (elaloumen) has been translated as an ingressive imperfect.
To the women. Apparently there were not enough Jews present in Philippi to have a synagogue (ten men would have been required to have one).
The word “there” is not in the Greek text, but is implied.

verses.zh: 有一个卖紫色布疋的妇人，名叫吕底亚，是推雅推喇城的人，素来敬拜　神。她听见了，主就开导她的心，叫她留心听保罗所讲的话。
verses.en: A[NOTE:1] woman named Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth[NOTE:2] from the city of Thyatira,[NOTE:3] a God-fearing woman, listened to us.[NOTE:4] The Lord opened her heart to respond[NOTE:5] to what Paul was saying.
notes: Grk “And a.” Because of the difference between Greek style, which often begins sentences or clauses with “and,” and English style, which generally does not, καί (kai) has not been translated here.
On the term translated “a dealer in purple cloth” see BDAG 855 s.v. πορφυρόπωλις.
Thyatira was a city in western Asia Minor.
The words “to us” are not in the Greek text, but are implied. Direct objects in Greek were often omitted when clear from the context, but must be supplied for the modern English reader.

Although BDAG 880 s.v. προσέχω 2.b gives the meaning “pay attention to” here, this could be misunderstood by the modern English reader to mean merely listening intently. The following context, however, indicates that Lydia responded positively to Paul’s message, so the verb here was translated “to respond.”sn Lydia is one of several significant women in Acts (see 17:4, 12, 34; 18:20).

verses.zh: 她和她一家既领了洗，便求我们说：「你们若以为我是真信主的（或译：你们若以为我是忠心事主的），请到我家里来住」；于是强留我们。
verses.en: After she and her household were baptized, she urged us,[NOTE:1] “If[NOTE:2] you consider me to be a believer in the Lord,[NOTE:3] come and stay in my house.” And she persuaded[NOTE:4] us.
notes: Grk “urged us, saying.” The participle λέγουσα (legousa) is redundant in English and has not been translated.
This is a first class condition in Greek, with the statement presented as real or true for the sake of the argument.

Or “faithful to the Lord.” BDAG 821 s.v. πίστος 2 states concerning this verse, “Of one who confesses the Christian faith believing or a believer in the Lord, in Christ, in God πιστ. τῷ κυρίῳ Ac 16:15.” L&N 11.17 has “one who is included among the faithful followers of Christ—‘believer, Christian, follower.’”
Although BDAG 759 s.v. παραβιάζομαι has “urge strongly, prevail upon,” in contemporary English “persuade” is a more frequently used synonym for “prevail upon.”

verses.zh: 后来，我们往那祷告的地方去。有一个使女迎着面来，她被巫鬼所附，用法术，叫她主人们大得财利。
verses.en: Now[NOTE:1] as we were going to the place of prayer, a slave girl met us who had a spirit that enabled her to foretell the future by supernatural means.[NOTE:2] She[NOTE:3] brought her owners[NOTE:4] a great profit by fortune-telling.[NOTE:5]
notes: Grk “Now it happened that.” The introductory phrase ἐγένετο (egeneto, “it happened that”), common in Luke (69 times) and Acts (54 times), is redundant in contemporary English and has not been translated.

Or “who had a spirit of divination”; Grk “who had a spirit of Python.” According to BDAG 896-97 s.v. πύθων, originally Πύθων (Puthōn) was the name of the serpent or dragon that guarded the Delphic oracle. According to Greek mythology, it lived at the foot of Mount Parnassus and was killed by Apollo. From this, the word came to designate a person who was thought to have a spirit of divination. Pagan generals, for example, might consult someone like this. So her presence here suggests a supernatural encounter involving Paul and her “spirit.” W. Foerster, TDNT 6:920, connects the term with ventriloquism but states: “We must assume, however, that for this girl, as for those mentioned by Origen…, the art of ventriloquism was inseparably connected with a (supposed or authentic) gift of soothsaying.” It should also be noted that if the girl in question here were only a ventriloquist, the exorcism performed by Paul in v. 18 would not have been effective.

Grk “who.” Because of the awkwardness in English of having two relative clauses follow one another (“who had a spirit…who brought her owners a great profit”) the relative pronoun here (“who”) has been translated as a pronoun (“she”) and a new sentence begun in the translation.
Or “masters.”
On this term see BDAG 616 s.v. μαντεύομαι. It was used of those who gave oracles.

verses.zh: 她跟随保罗和我们，喊着说：「这些人是至高　神的仆人，对你们传说救人的道。」
verses.en: She followed behind Paul and us and kept crying out,[NOTE:1] “These men are servants[NOTE:2] of the Most High God, who are proclaiming to you the way[NOTE:3] of salvation.”[NOTE:4]
notes: Grk “crying out, saying”; the participle λέγουσα (legousa) is redundant in English and has not been translated. The imperfect verb ἔκραζεν (ekrazen) has been translated as a progressive imperfect.

Grk “slaves.” See the note on the word “servants” in 2:18. The translation “servants” was used here because in this context there appears to be more emphasis on the activity of Paul and his companions (“proclaiming to you the way of salvation”) than on their status as “slaves of the Most High God.”

Or “a way.” The grammar of this phrase is a bit ambiguous. The phrase in Greek is ὁδὸν σωτηρίας (hodon sōtērias). Neither the head noun nor the genitive noun has the article; this is in keeping with Apollonius’ Canon (see ExSyn 239-40). Since both nouns are anarthrous, this construction also fits Apollonius’ Corollary (see ExSyn 250-54); since the genitive noun is abstract it is most naturally qualitative, so the head noun could either be definite or indefinite without being unusual as far as the grammar is concerned. Luke’s usage of ὁδός elsewhere is indecisive as far as this passage is concerned. However, when one looks at the historical background it is clear that (1) the woman is shut up (via exorcism) not because her testimony is false but because of its source (analogous to Jesus’ treatment of demons perhaps), and (b) “the way” is a par excellence description of the new faith throughout Acts. It thus seems that at least in Luke’s presentation “the way of salvation” is the preferred translation.

Proclaiming to you the way of salvation. The remarks were an ironic recognition of Paul’s authority, but he did not desire such a witness, possibly for fear of confusion. Her expression the Most High God might have been understood as Zeus by the audience.

verses.zh: 她一连多日这样喊叫，保罗就心中厌烦，转身对那鬼说：「我奉耶稣基督的名，吩咐你从她身上出来！」那鬼当时就出来了。
verses.en: She continued to do this for many days. But Paul became greatly annoyed,[NOTE:1] and turned[NOTE:2] and said to the spirit, “I command you in the name of Jesus Christ[NOTE:3] to come out of her!” And it came out of her at once.[NOTE:4]
notes: Grk “becoming greatly annoyed.” The participle διαπονηθείς (diaponētheis) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style. The aorist has been translated as an ingressive aorist (entry into a state or condition). See BDAG 235 s.v. διαπονέομαι.
Grk “and turning.” The participle ἐπιστρέψας (epistrepsas) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style.
Or “Messiah”; both “Christ” (Greek) and “Messiah” (Hebrew and Aramaic) mean “one who has been anointed.”
BDAG 1102-3 s.v. ὥρα 2.c has “at that very time, at once, instantly” for the usage in this verse.

verses.zh: 使女的主人们见得利的指望没有了，便揪住保罗和西拉，拉他们到市上去见首领；
verses.en: But when her owners[NOTE:1] saw their hope of profit[NOTE:2] was gone, they seized[NOTE:3] Paul and Silas and dragged[NOTE:4] them into the marketplace[NOTE:5] before the authorities.
notes: Or “masters.”
On this use of ἐργασία (ergasia), see BDAG 390 s.v. 4. It is often the case that destructive practices and commerce are closely tied together.
Grk “was gone, seizing.” The participle ἐπιλαβόμενοι (epilabomenoi) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style.
On the term ἕλκω (helkō) see BDAG 318 s.v. 1.

The marketplace (Greek agora) was not only a place of trade and commerce in the first century Greco-Roman world. It was a place of discussion and dialogue (the “public square”), a place of judgment (courts held session there), a place for idle people and those seeking work, and a place for children to play.

verses.zh: 又带到官长面前说：「这些人原是犹太人，竟骚扰我们的城，
verses.en: When[NOTE:1] they had brought them[NOTE:2] before the magistrates, they said, “These men are throwing our city into confusion.[NOTE:3] They are[NOTE:4] Jews
notes: Grk “And when.” Because of the difference between Greek style, which often begins sentences or clauses with “and,” and English style, which generally does not, καί (kai) has not been translated here.

Grk “having brought them.” The participle ἐπιλαβόμενοι (epilabomenoi) has been taken temporally. It is also possible in English to translate this participle as a finite verb: “they brought them before the magistrates and said.”
BDAG 309 s.v. ἐκταράσσω has “agitate, cause trouble to, throw into confusion” for the meaning of this verb.
Grk “being Jews, and they are proclaiming.” The participle ὑπάρχοντες (huparchontes) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style.

verses.zh: 传我们罗马人所不可受不可行的规矩。」
verses.en: and are advocating[NOTE:1] customs that are not lawful for us to accept[NOTE:2] or practice,[NOTE:3] since we are[NOTE:4] Romans.”
notes: Grk “proclaiming,” but in relation to customs, “advocating” is a closer approximation to the meaning.
Or “acknowledge.”

Customs that are not lawful for us to accept or practice. Ironically, the charges are similar to those made against Jesus in Luke 23:2, where Jews argued he was “twisting” their customs. The charge has three elements: (1) a racial element (Jewish); (2) a social element (unlawful); and (3) a traditional element (not their customs).
Grk “we being Romans.” The participle οὖσιν (ousin) has been translated as a causal adverbial participle.

verses.zh: 众人就一同起来攻击他们。官长吩咐剥了他们的衣裳，用棍打；
verses.en: The crowd joined the attack[NOTE:1] against them, and the magistrates tore the clothes[NOTE:2] off Paul and Silas[NOTE:3] and ordered them to be beaten with rods.[NOTE:4]
notes: L&N 39.50 has “the crowd joined the attack against them” for συνεπέστη (sunepestē) in this verse.

Grk “tearing the clothes off them, the magistrates ordered.” The participle περιρήξαντες (perirēxantes) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style. Although it may be possible to understand the aorist active participle περιρήξαντες in a causative sense (“the magistrates caused the clothes to be torn off Paul and Silas”) in the mob scene that was taking place, it is also possible that the magistrates themselves actively participated. This act was done to prepare them for a public flogging (2 Cor 11:25; 1 Thess 2:2).
Grk “off them”; the referents (Paul and Silas) have been specified in the translation for clarity.
The infinitive ῥαβδίζειν (rhabdizein) means “to beat with rods or sticks” (as opposed to fists, BDAG 902 s.v. ῥαβδίζω).

verses.zh: 打了许多棍，便将他们下在监里，嘱咐禁卒严紧看守。
verses.en: After they had beaten them severely,[NOTE:1] they threw them into prison and commanded[NOTE:2] the jailer to guard them securely.
notes: Grk “Having inflicted many blows on them.” The participle ἐπιθέντες (epithentes) has been taken temporally. BDAG 384 s.v. ἐπιτίθημι 1.a.β has “inflict blows upon someone” for this expression, but in this context it is simpler to translate in English as “they had beaten them severely.”
Grk “commanding.” The participle παραγγείλαντες (parangeilantes) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style.

verses.zh: 禁卒领了这样的命，就把他们下在内监里，两脚上了木狗。
verses.en: Receiving such orders, he threw them in the inner cell[NOTE:1] and fastened their feet in the stocks.[NOTE:2]
notes: Or “prison.”

L&N 6.21 has “stocks” for εἰς τὸ ξύλον (eis to xulon) here, as does BDAG 685 s.v. ξύλον 2.b. However, it is also possible (as mentioned in L&N 18.12) that this does not mean “stocks” but a block of wood (a log or wooden column) in the prison to which prisoners’ feet were chained or tied. Such a possibility is suggested by v. 26, where the “bonds” (“chains”?) of the prisoners loosened.

verses.zh: 约在半夜，保罗和西拉祷告，唱诗赞美　神，众囚犯也侧耳而听。
verses.en: About midnight Paul and Silas were praying[NOTE:1] and singing hymns to God,[NOTE:2] and the rest of[NOTE:3] the prisoners were listening to them.
notes: Grk “praying, were singing.” The participle προσευχόμενοι (proseuchomenoi) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style.

Praying and singing hymns to God. Tertullian said, “The legs feel nothing in the stocks when the heart is in heaven” (To the Martyrs 2; cf. Rom 5:3; Jas 1:2; 1 Pet 5:6). The presence of God means the potential to be free (cf. v. 26).
The words “the rest of” are not in the Greek text, but are implied.

verses.zh: 忽然，地大震动，甚至监牢的地基都摇动了，监门立刻全开，众囚犯的锁链也都松开了。
verses.en: Suddenly a great earthquake occurred, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken. Immediately all the doors flew open, and the bonds[NOTE:1] of all the prisoners came loose.
notes: Or perhaps, “chains.” The translation of τὰ δεσμά (ta desma) is to some extent affected by the understanding of ξύλον (xulon, “stocks”) in v. 24. It is possible (as mentioned in L&N 18.12) that this does not mean “stocks” but a block of wood (a log or wooden column) in the prison to which prisoners’ feet were chained or tied.

verses.zh: 禁卒一醒，看见监门全开，以为囚犯已经逃走，就拔刀要自杀。
verses.en: When the jailer woke up[NOTE:1] and saw the doors of the prison standing open,[NOTE:2] he drew his sword and was about to kill himself[NOTE:3] because he assumed[NOTE:4] the prisoners had escaped.
notes: L&N 23.75 has “had awakened” here. It is more in keeping with contemporary English style, however, to keep the two verbal ideas parallel in terms of tense (“when the jailer woke up and saw”) although logically the second action is subsequent to the first.
The additional semantic component “standing” is supplied (“standing open”) to convey a stative nuance in English.
Was about to kill himself. The jailer’s penalty for failing to guard the prisoners would have been death, so he contemplated saving the leaders the trouble (see Acts 12:19; 27:42).
Or “thought.”

verses.zh: 保罗大声呼叫说：「不要伤害自己！我们都在这里。」
verses.en: But Paul called out loudly,[NOTE:1] “Do not harm yourself,[NOTE:2] for we are all here!”
notes: Grk “But Paul called out with a loud voice, saying.” The dative phrase μεγάλῃ φωνῇ (megalē phōnē) has been simplified as an English adverb (“loudly”), and the participle λέγων (legōn) has not been translated since it is redundant in English.
Do not harm yourself. Again the irony is that Paul is the agent through whom the jailer is spared.

verses.zh: 禁卒叫人拿灯来，就跳进去，战战兢兢地俯伏在保罗、西拉面前；
verses.en: Calling for lights, the jailer[NOTE:1] rushed in and fell down[NOTE:2] trembling at the feet of Paul and Silas.
notes: Grk “he”; the referent (the jailer) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

Fell down. The earthquake and the freeing of the prisoners showed that God’s power was present. Such power could only be recognized. The open doors opened the jailer’s heart.tn Or “and prostrated himself.”

verses.zh: 又领他们出来，说：「二位先生，我当怎样行才可以得救？」
verses.en: Then he brought them outside[NOTE:1] and asked, “Sirs, what must[NOTE:2] I do to be saved?”
notes: Grk “And bringing them outside, he asked.” The participle προαγαγών (proagagōn) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style. Because of the length of the Greek sentence, the conjunction καί (kai) has not been translated here. Instead a new English sentence is begun by supplying the conjunction “then” to indicate the logical sequence.
The Greek term (δεῖ, dei) is used by Luke to represent divine necessity.

verses.zh: 他们说：「当信主耶稣，你和你一家都必得救。」
verses.en: They replied,[NOTE:1] “Believe[NOTE:2] in the Lord Jesus[NOTE:3] and you will be saved, you and your household.”
notes: Grk “said.”
Here the summary term of response is a call to believe. In this context it refers to trusting the sovereign God’s power to deliver, which events had just pictured for the jailer.

The majority of mss add Χριστόν (Christon, “Christ”) here (C D E Ψ 1739 M sy sa), but the best and earliest witnesses read simply τὸν κύριον ᾿Ιησοῦν (ton kurion Iēsoun, “the Lord Jesus”; P74vid א A B 33 81 bo). The addition of “Christ” to “Lord Jesus” is an obviously motivated reading. Thus on both external and internal grounds, the shorter reading is strongly preferred.

verses.zh: 他们就把主的道讲给他和他全家的人听。
verses.en: Then[NOTE:1] they spoke the word of the Lord[NOTE:2] to him, along with all those who were in his house.
notes: Grk “And they.” Here καί (kai) has been translated as “then” to indicate the continuity with the preceding verse. Greek style often begins sentences or clauses with “and,” but English style does not.

The word of the Lord is a technical expression in OT literature, often referring to a divine prophetic utterance (e.g., Gen 15:1, Isa 1:10, Jonah 1:1). In the NT it occurs 15 times: 3 times as ῥῆμα τοῦ κυρίου (rhēma tou kuriou; Luke 22:61, Acts 11:16, 1 Pet 1:25) and 12 times as λόγος τοῦ κυρίου (logos tou kuriou; here and in Acts 8:25; 13:44, 48, 49; 15:35, 36; 19:10, 20; 1 Thess 1:8; 4:15; 2 Thess 3:1). As in the OT, this phrase focuses on the prophetic nature and divine origin of what has been said.

verses.zh: 当夜，就在那时候，禁卒把他们带去，洗他们的伤；他和属乎他的人立时都受了洗。
verses.en: At[NOTE:1] that hour of the night he took them[NOTE:2] and washed their wounds;[NOTE:3] then[NOTE:4] he and all his family[NOTE:5] were baptized right away.[NOTE:6]
notes: Grk “And at.” Because of the difference between Greek style, which often begins sentences or clauses with “and,” and English style, which generally does not, καί (kai) has not been translated here.
Grk “taking them…he washed.” The participle παραλαβών (paralabōn) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style.
On this phrase BDAG 603 s.v. λούω 1 gives a literal translation as “by washing he freed them from the effects of the blows.”
Here καί (kai) has been translated as “then” to indicate the logical sequence.
All his family. It was often the case in the ancient world that conversion of the father led to the conversion of all those in the household.
Or “immediately.”

verses.zh: 于是禁卒领他们上自己家里去，给他们摆上饭。他和全家，因为信了　神，都很喜乐。
verses.en: The jailer[NOTE:1] brought them into his house and set food[NOTE:2] before them, and he rejoiced greatly[NOTE:3] that he had come to believe[NOTE:4] in God, together with his entire household.[NOTE:5]
notes: Grk “He”; the referent (the jailer) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

Grk “placed [food] on the table” (a figurative expression). Since the actual word for food is not specified, it would also be possible to translate “set a meal before them,” but since this is taking place in the middle of the night, the preparations necessary for a full meal would probably not have been made. More likely Paul and Silas were given whatever was on hand that needed little or no preparation.
Or “he was overjoyed.”
The translation “come to believe” reflects more of the resultative nuance of the perfect tense here.

The phrase “together with his entire household” is placed at the end of the English sentence so that it refers to both the rejoicing and the belief. A formal equivalence translation would have “and he rejoiced greatly with his entire household that he had come to believe in God,” but the reference to the entire household being baptized in v. 33 presumes that all in the household believed.

verses.zh: 到了天亮，官长打发差役来，说：「释放那两个人吧。」
verses.en: At daybreak[NOTE:1] the magistrates[NOTE:2] sent their police officers,[NOTE:3] saying, “Release those men.”
notes: The translation “day is breaking” for ἡμέρα γίνεται (hēmera ginetai) in this verse is given by BDAG 436 s.v. ἡμέρα 1.a.

On the term translated “magistrates,” see BDAG 947-48 s.v. στρατηγός 1. These city leaders were properly called duoviri, but were popularly known as praetors (στρατηγοί, stratēgoi). They were the chief officials of Philippi. The text leaves the impression that they came to the decision to release Paul and Silas independently. God was at work everywhere.
On the term ῥαβδοῦχος (rhabdouchos) see BDAG 902 s.v. The term was used of the Roman lictor and roughly corresponds to contemporary English “constable, policeman.”

verses.zh: 禁卒就把这话告诉保罗说：「官长打发人来叫释放你们，如今可以出监，平平安安地去吧。」
verses.en: The jailer reported these words to Paul, saying,[NOTE:1] “The magistrates have sent orders[NOTE:2] to release you. So come out now and go in peace.”[NOTE:3]
notes: The word “saying” is not in the Greek text, but is implied; it is necessary in English because the content of what the jailer said to Paul and Silas is not the exact message related to him by the police officers, but is a summary with his own additions.
The word “orders” is not in the Greek text, but is implied. Direct objects in Greek were often omitted when clear from the context, but must be supplied for the modern English reader.
Grk “So coming out now go in peace.” The participle ἐξελθόντες (exelthontes) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style.

verses.zh: 保罗却说：「我们是罗马人，并没有定罪，他们就在众人面前打了我们，又把我们下在监里，现在要私下撵我们出去吗？这是不行的。叫他们自己来领我们出去吧！」
verses.en: But Paul said to the police officers,[NOTE:1] “They had us beaten in public[NOTE:2] without a proper trial[NOTE:3]—even though we are Roman citizens[NOTE:4]—and they threw us[NOTE:5] in prison. And now they want to send us away[NOTE:6] secretly? Absolutely not! They[NOTE:7] themselves must come and escort us out!”[NOTE:8]
notes: Grk “to them”; the referent (the police officers) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Grk “Having us beaten in public.” The participle δείραντες (deirantes) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style.
Or “in public, uncondemned.” BDAG 35 s.v. ἀκατάκριτος has “uncondemned, without due process” for this usage.
The participle ὑπάρχοντας (huparchontas) has been translated as a concessive adverbial participle.
The word “us” is not in the Greek text, but is implied. Direct objects were often omitted in Greek when clear from the context, but must be supplied for the modern English reader.
L&N 28.71 has “send us away secretly” for this verse.
Grk “But they.”

They themselves must come and escort us out! Paul was asking for the injustice he and Silas suffered to be symbolically righted. It was a way of publicly taking their actions off the record and showing the apostles’ innocence, a major public statement. Note the apology given in v. 39.

verses.zh: 差役把这话回禀官长。官长听见他们是罗马人，就害怕了，
verses.en: The police officers reported these words to the magistrates. They were frightened when they heard Paul and Silas[NOTE:1] were Roman citizens[NOTE:2]
notes: Grk “heard they”; the referents (Paul and Silas) have been specified in the translation for clarity.

Roman citizens. This fact was disturbing to the officials because due process was a right for a Roman citizen, well established in Roman law. To flog a Roman citizen was considered an abomination. Such punishment was reserved for noncitizens.

verses.zh: 于是来劝他们，领他们出来，请他们离开那城。
verses.en: and came[NOTE:1] and apologized to them. After[NOTE:2] they brought them out, they asked them repeatedly[NOTE:3] to leave the city.
notes: Grk “and coming, they apologized.” The participle ἐλθόντες (elthontes) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style.
Grk “and after.” Because of the length of the Greek sentence, the conjunction καί (kai) has not been translated here. Instead a new English sentence is begun.
The verb ἐρώτων (erōtōn) has been translated as an iterative imperfect; the English adverb “repeatedly” brings out the iterative force in the translation.

verses.zh: 二人出了监，往吕底亚家里去，见了弟兄们，劝慰他们一番，就走了。
verses.en: When they came out of the prison, they entered Lydia’s house, and when they saw the brothers, they encouraged them and then[NOTE:1] departed.
notes: “Then” is not in the Greek text, but has been supplied to clarify the logical sequence in the translation.
